title: Municipal Trade Crews as Robot Training Data
one_liner: A cooperative that licenses consented, privacy-scrubbed first-person footage of city public-works and utility crews doing real skilled work to robotics labs, with revenue shared to the city and the union's training fund.
customer: Robotics foundation-model labs and robot-data buyers pay per usable hour (Physical Intelligence-class labs, XDOF, Mecka). The supply side is public works departments, transit maintenance shops and public-sector union locals (AFSCME, IBEW), which receive a 40-50% share.
problem: The humanoid bottleneck is a 'dearth of physical-world data'. Robot-data startups pay people to film themselves making coffee or fixing cars (XDOF at about $50M annualized revenue three months out of stealth, Mecka projecting $100M ARR). Those demos are shallow next to expert skilled-trade work in messy environments: valve exercising, hydrant flushing, pothole patching, streetlight repair, sewer inspection. Cities meanwhile face tight budgets and need non-tax revenue.
solution: Equip volunteer crews with head cameras and simple sensors for specified tasks. Scrub faces and license plates on-device, label task steps, and license clean hours under a contract in which the city retains ownership. Worker pay per hour and a union-controlled training fund keep labor onside. Later, offer 'task-specific corpora' by trade (electrical, plumbing, HVAC) via apprenticeship programs.
why_now: Robot foundation models raised at $3-14B valuations in 2026 and are starved for data. Data-as-a-service is the hot new category (XDOF, Mecka). The humanoid shipment wave (about 22,000 in H1 2026) creates immediate demand. Cities are under budget pressure (Maryland's new IT tax raised 77% less than projected).
revenue_model: Data licensing per usable hour and per task-specific corpus, with 40-50% of revenue shared to the city and union training fund. Enterprise annual data licenses for labs.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input for physical AI is expert skilled-trades demonstrations, and public works departments and their unions are the only large organized pools of trained workers with a single governance body that can sign one contract. Paying the workers and the union turns what looks like 'training your replacement' into a data dividend.
first_30_days: Find one mid-size public works department and one union local. Run a 10-worker, 2-week pilot with head cameras on two task types. Sell the first 300-500 cleaned hours to one robotics lab and pay the crews and training fund on the first invoice.

title: Buyout Bridge for Flood-Prone Counties
one_liner: Run the paperwork of county flood buyouts and front cash to owners, reimbursed when grants land.
customer: County and municipal floodplain managers and state hazard-mitigation offices, paying from program administration budgets. Later, impact and philanthropic capital for the bridge fund.
problem: Risk Rating 2.0 pushes premiums toward full risk (median $689 versus about $1,288 needed, per CRS, secondary source), eroding equity in repeatedly flooded homes. Owners want out, but FEMA programs are erratic: BRIC was cancelled in April 2025, restored by court order and reinstated Mar 18 2026, with applications closed July 23 2026. Buyouts take years, so owners sit in limbo or sell at fire-sale prices.
solution: An operations and software backbone for county acquisition programs: eligibility, duplication-of-benefits tracking, appraisal, title, relocation counseling, demolition procurement, open-space deed restrictions and reimbursement compliance. Then add a pooled bridge fund that pays owners in 60-90 days and is repaid from grants.
why_now: The NFIP glide path to full-risk pricing, plus the BRIC cancel-and-restore whiplash, leaves states building their own programs.
revenue_model: $3-8K fixed admin fee per acquisition, and later a bridge-loan spread.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not money but cash timing and paperwork, and governments will pay for throughput more readily than for software.
first_30_days: Pick 3 counties with repetitive-loss acquisition backlogs and offer to run 20 properties under a $25K pilot. Publish time-to-close as the benchmark.

title: Fixed-Price MDR Clinical Evaluation Reports via ASReview
one_liner: A tech-enabled service that uses the open-source ASReview active-learning screener plus medical writers to deliver audit-ready literature-based Clinical Evaluation Reports at a fraction of consultant prices.
customer: EU MDR device makers with 5-50 staff: digital-health and software-as-a-medical-device startups, legacy Class I/IIa/IIb device makers, and regulatory consultants who need white-label capacity.
problem: MDR requires a Clinical Evaluation Report built on a systematic literature review with appraisal, state-of-the-art analysis and ongoing updates. Consultants charge roughly EUR 10-40k for a literature-based CER. Small firms delay certification or withdraw legacy products because of clinical-evaluation cost.
solution: Run the search protocol in PubMed and other open sources, ClinicalTrials.gov and vigilance databases. Screen with ASReview LAB (validated in Nature Machine Intelligence) with the full screening log retained. A medical writer and a clinical expert appraise and sign off. Deliver the CER plus a PRISMA-style flow diagram and search-string appendix, then sell a quarterly 'living' update for post-market clinical follow-up.
why_now: Legacy-device MDR transition deadlines fall in 2027-2028 and notified-body capacity is tight. Half of medtechs report expecting to spend 5% or more of revenue on MDR. ASReview is mature and widely used in academia, but no one packages it for regulatory work.
revenue_model: Fixed fee of EUR 4-9k per literature-based CER on low-risk devices. Recurring literature-update subscriptions of EUR 1.2-3k per year. Wholesale white-label pricing for consultancies.
non_obvious_insight: Notified bodies rarely reject a CER because the science is thin. They reject it because the methodology is undocumented: search protocol, appraisal criteria, equivalence reasoning. ASReview's transparent, reproducible logging is the compliance artifact, so sell reproducibility rather than speed.
first_30_days: Recruit two freelance medical writers and one clinician-reviewer. Publish three sample CER sections for a public device category as proof. Post in regulatory-affairs communities (RAPS chapters, MDR LinkedIn groups). Sell the first five CERs at a design-partner price and use the audit trail from each as the case study.

title: Proctored Truth Audits for School Edtech
one_liner: Short, paper-based, device-free probes that tell districts whether the practice software they license teaches anything, now that AI can do the practice for the child.
customer: District curriculum and assessment directors (5k-50k student districts) that renew six-figure math/ELA practice licenses; secondary: charter networks. Edtech vendors are a later, firewalled buyer of verified listings.
problem: Practice dashboards show rising accuracy, but ALEKS data (June 2026 working paper, not peer-reviewed) show proctored word-problem accuracy falling from about 80% to about 60% after ChatGPT while unsupervised accuracy rose. A 2-year Tennessee study found Khanmigo added nothing over Khan Academy alone. Districts renew on usage and mastery metrics that AI now contaminates.
solution: Twenty-minute proctored paper probes at the start, middle and end of term, on a random sample of classrooms, aligned to the same standards as the platform and including graphing items that are hard to paste into AI. Human-scored from scans. Output is a per-product, per-school report: what share of platform 'mastery' survives an unassisted check, and cost per verified mastery. Later, a benchmark vendors pay to be listed on.
why_now: Unsupervised practice data has visibly decoupled from learning (2026 ALEKS study). ESSER money is gone, so renewals get scrutiny. NYC and LAUSD paused AI for 2026-27, and boards now want proof. Over half of teachers say AI harms critical thinking.
revenue_model: Annual district audit contracts of $15k-60k per product per grade band, plus per-school scanning and scoring fees. Later, vendor-funded verification listings kept separate from the audit results.
non_obvious_insight: When students can outsource practice, engagement and accuracy metrics measure the AI, not the child. The only trustworthy learning data is now scarce, unassisted and physical, so the measurement layer, not the content layer, becomes the moat.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 curriculum directors who are mid-renewal fight. Run a free 6-classroom pilot with paper probes built from released state-test items plus hand-drawn graphing items. Have a few retired teachers score them. Hand over a 2-page usage-versus-learning report before their renewal decision, then convert to a $15-25k paid audit.

title: Heat and Smoke Stop-Day Kit for Outdoor Crews
one_liner: Text-message heat and smoke compliance for small outdoor employers, sold through comp carriers and PEOs, with parametric stop-day cover to follow.
customer: Workers' comp carriers and PEOs serving small landscapers, roofers, framers and farms in California, Washington and Oregon (later AZ, TX, CO), plus general contractors that need subs' plans.
problem: OSHA's federal heat rule has slipped (supplemental proposal Dec 2026, final Oct 2027), but California, Washington and Oregon already bind employers. Small crews have no written plan, acclimatization tracking or go/no-go rule. Heat and smoke stop-work days hurt small-contractor cash flow, and business-interruption cover for them is barely productized.
solution: Phase one is a text-message-first kit: site-level heat and air-quality alerts, a state-specific written plan, water, shade and break logs, acclimatization schedules and audit exports. Phase two adds parametric stop-day cover through an MGA partner, with WBGT or AQI triggers.
why_now: The summer 2026 shock and state rules make compliance urgent, while federal delay pushes pressure onto carriers and GCs.
revenue_model: $39-99 per crew per month, or per-employee fees from carriers and PEOs for loss control, plus parametric premium margin later.
non_obvious_insight: Demand does not depend on OSHA. States, general-contractor prequalification and comp-carrier loss control drive it.
first_30_days: Pitch two comp-carrier loss-control teams and a landscaping association. Run a 20-crew pilot with the plan generator and alerts.

title: Chain-of-Custody Certificates for Spent PFAS Media
one_liner: A broker and tracking service that consolidates spent GAC and ion-exchange media from small utilities, routes it to verified destruction, and issues auditable certificates that document where the waste went.
customer: Small and mid-size water systems that have installed or are installing PFAS treatment, plus the treatment vendors and engineers who can bundle the service. Utilities pay per ton, and vendors pay referral fees.
problem: Step one: the 4 ppt PFOA/PFOS limits stand, monitoring is due in 2027 and compliance is proposed for 2031. Step two: treatment media saturates and must be replaced every one to three years. Step three: landfills increasingly refuse it, destruction capacity is thin, and utilities fear long-tail liability (PFOA and PFOS were designated CERCLA hazardous substances in 2024, from my background knowledge). The brief flags disposal as a downstream bottleneck but it is unverified.
solution: Start as a broker: aggregate small batches into full loads, match them to thermal reactivation, high-temperature incineration or newer destruction technologies, and issue a standard 'certificate of destruction' with custody records (tagged bulk bags, manifests, destruction-efficiency evidence and insurance). Sell it to media vendors as a bundled add-on. Later, add software for utilities' liability files.
why_now: Utilities that installed treatment after state limits and settlement money (3M and DuPont) are now hitting first change-outs. The delay from 2029 to 2031 moves the compliance date but not the disposal-liability clock.
revenue_model: 15-25% margin on disposal contracts ($ per ton), annual custody-software subscription and insurance-backed certificate fees.
non_obvious_insight: Regulatory relief changes when utilities must install treatment, not who owns the waste after it is installed. Buyers want absolution and paperwork more than the cheapest disposal, so documentation and insurance are the product.
first_30_days: Identify 10-20 utilities with early PFAS installs and imminent media change-outs from state announcements. Interview two disposal handlers and one reactivation vendor. Have an environmental attorney review a certificate template. Sign three pilot loads.

title: Two A.M. Any-Tradition Rites and Interpreter Line
one_liner: A 24/7 dispatch of vetted ritual specialists and death-trained interpreters for families outside the majority faith, sold to hospices and palliative units.
customer: Hospices, hospital palliative units and nursing homes in metros with large immigrant and non-Christian populations. They pay a monthly retainer plus per-dispatch fees.
problem: Most hospice chaplains are generalists trained in a Christian or interfaith pastoral model, and chaplain FTEs are among the first things cut when margins tighten. When an imam, Hindu priest, Buddhist monk, Sikh granthi, Hmong ritual specialist, Orthodox priest, or Native elder is needed, the family often gets the default chaplain, and the ritual windows are short and unforgiving. Some rites happen only before death, others require that the body not be moved or touched for hours, or that someone be present continuously. Standard hospice protocol says 'call the funeral home now.' Language is the second failure. Family members interpret for the patient and quietly soften bad news. In many languages the word 'dying' is unsayable. Interpreter contracts are priced per minute and built for clinic visits, with no death vocabulary or truth-telling norm training.
solution: A dispatch line and app for the hospice chaplain or on-call nurse. It connects to a vetted, paid roster of ritual specialists by tradition and language who can arrive or join by video, plus a small pool of interpreters who have completed a 40-hour end-of-life interpreting course (death vocabulary, family-filtering, cultural norms about naming prognosis). A one-page 'rite card' library is loaded into the hospice's EHR or intranet for each tradition. It gives the practical do's and don'ts: how to position the patient, what not to do to the body, who should not touch it, how long to wait before calling the funeral home, and what the family may ask for. Start with one metro and 4 to 6 traditions.
why_now: AI translation is tempting hospices to cut interpreter budgets, while civil-rights language-access rules (Section 1557 of the ACA as revised in 2024) push toward qualified interpreters and human review of machine translation for critical content. Confirm the current status of those rules. The older-adult population is more foreign-born and religiously diverse than a decade ago, and the unaffiliated 'nones' need secular rituals too. Chaplain staffing is shrinking. Consolidated hospice chains want scalable ways to meet 'emotional and spiritual support' quality measures.
revenue_model: A monthly retainer of $1,500 to $4,000 per hospice or hospital for 24/7 access. Per-dispatch fees ($150 to $300 to the specialist, with a 30 to 40 percent platform margin). Premium per-minute interpreting rates above standard telephone rates. Training and certification revenue from the interpreter course, sold to language-service companies and hospitals. Family fees are not charged.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing is not spiritual care in general but time-critical, tradition-specific competence at the exact hour of death, which a generalist chaplain honestly cannot supply. Family interpreters are the largest hidden source of bad-news distortion in end-of-life care. Whoever builds the roster and the interpreter standard owns a moat that AI translation cannot cross, because the value is trust and ritual authority, not words.
first_30_days: Pick one metro where you know the communities (for example Minneapolis–St. Paul for Hmong, Somali and Karen families, or Houston or Queens for a wider mix). Recruit 20 to 25 ritual specialists and interpreters through mosque, temple and community boards, and pay them a small stipend for a 3-hour training on hospice basics. Build the rite-card library with their input. Sign two hospices to a free 60-day pilot on a shared phone number, then convert them to a retainer and use their case counts in a pitch to the next five.

title: Size Ladder: Circular Wardrobes for GLP-1 Users
one_liner: A subscription that ships the next clothing size on the GLP-1 titration schedule, takes back the last, stores a 'restart' wardrobe, and routes the excess into resale and recycling, sold through telehealth partners as a retention perk.
customer: Cash-pay GLP-1 patients ($59-129 a month), telehealth and clinic operators paying a per-member fee for retention, and plus-size apparel brands and textile-EPR schemes that need diverted volume.
problem: Users move through three to five sizes in 12-18 months, and only about a third are still on therapy at one year while roughly 60% of ex-users plan to restart and stoppers regain about two thirds within a year. So closets fill with clothes that fit neither the current body nor the likely future one. The US textile recycling rate is 14.7% and California alone landfills 1.2M tons a year. Telehealth players have converged on the same $149-$349 price, so they need non-price loyalty features.
solution: At each dose step or every 10 lb, ship the next size from a pooled inventory of pre-owned and new pieces, take back the previous size, and offer take-in tailoring as an alternative. A 'restart wardrobe' bank holds the prior size for 12 months for a small fee. With consent, the telehealth partner shares titration stage so the platform can forecast sizes; in return the clinician sees a behavioral signal when size changes stall or reverse.
why_now: Cash-pay pills at $149 have widened the user base (22% of households have a user) and moved buying away from insurers to consumers who are already spending more on skincare and fragrance. California's textile EPR (SB 707) is moving toward fee-setting, creating a funded outlet for take-back volume. Compounding's exit has pushed users onto branded cash-pay channels that want stickiness.
revenue_model: Consumer subscription, partner PMPM fees ($3-6) from telehealth for retention, brand sponsorship from apparel companies, and resale margin plus EPR diversion credits on the outflow.
non_obvious_insight: Titration is a clock. Because dose steps predict weight-loss milestones, the apparel demand curve is forecastable in a way no fashion category ever is, and the closet is the earliest behavioral read-out of regain.
first_30_days: Recruit 50 patients from GLP-1 patient communities and one partner clinic. Source pre-owned plus-size inventory cheaply from thrift and textile sorters. Line up a tailor network. Run a 3-month pilot at $79 a month, tracking return rates, size churn and how well titration stage predicts the next size.

title: Cool-Cap Ledger: Indoor Temperature Evidence for Landlords
one_liner: Low-cost sensors and tamper-evident logs that give landlords, tenants and inspectors one accepted reading of indoor temperature.
customer: Owners and property managers of 10+ unit buildings in Maryland (80F cap since June 1 2026), LA County (82F from Jan 1 2027) and NYC (78F cap, owner duty from 2030). Tenant groups and code enforcement are secondary buyers.
problem: Cooling caps are enforced by complaint, so the fight will be over readings: a tenant's phone app against a landlord with no record. Landlords face fines and habitability suits with no defensible data, and tenants cannot prove violations.
solution: $30 sensors in a sampled set of units, third-party-verifiable logs, a tenant-visible dashboard, automated compliance reports and a dispute-response pack. An upsell is a unit-level cooling-gap map for capex planning, showing which units to retrofit first under LA County's phase-in.
why_now: Maryland's cap is already live, LA County starts in about 3 months, and NYC Local Law 2026/023 is passed. The summer 2026 heat set off a wave of complaints.
revenue_model: $4-8 per unit per month for landlords, plus municipal enforcement licenses.
non_obvious_insight: In a complaint-driven regime, evidence is the product. Neutral data protects landlords from false claims and tenants from real violations, so both sides will accept it.
first_30_days: Sign 5-10 LA County and Maryland property managers for winter pilots ahead of the Jan 2027 start. Build the logging and report pack, and pilot in 100 units.

title: Closing-Time Recovery for Shutting Small Businesses
one_liner: A contingency-fee agent that finds and collects the money owners forget when they close: tariff refunds, overpaid taxes, insurance returns, deposits and vendor credits.
customer: Owners of small businesses closing or filing Chapter 7 or Subchapter V (restaurants, boutique importers, e-commerce brands, agencies), plus trustees and wind-down lawyers who will not chase small assets.
problem: Exhausted owners walk away from uncollected money. Customs owes about $166B in IEEPA tariff refunds to roughly 330,000 importers after the Supreme Court struck the tariffs down on February 20, 2026, with refunds running through CBP's CAPE portal and protest windows expiring on a rolling basis. Beyond tariffs, there are overpaid sales and payroll taxes, unearned insurance premium, utility and landlord deposits, vendor credits, customer deposits, workers' comp dividends and unclaimed property. Trustees often skip small claims because the cost outweighs the return.
solution: Run a standard 40-item recovery checklist automatically: pull entry data through a licensed customs-broker partner with a power of attorney, search unclaimed property, send insurer audit and refund requests, and file claims with a partner wind-down attorney. Find leads from PACER filings, state dissolution records, lien releases, landlords and accountants. Take 20-30% of recovered funds and pay nothing if nothing is found.
why_now: Tariff refunds are moving but the deadlines to claim them are rolling off. Higher rates, the energy shock and squeezed lower-income consumers are pushing more small businesses to close. Contingency-fee legal and customs partners are available and CBP now has a digital claim channel.
revenue_model: 20-30% contingency on recovered amounts, with typical finds of $8-40k per closing business. Referral fees from trustees and lawyers.
non_obvious_insight: The biggest asset in a dying small business is often not equipment but claims against governments and vendors the owner does not know exist. A closing owner has no bandwidth, so willingness to hand over a percentage is high, and the funnel widens in every downturn.
first_30_days: Partner with one wind-down attorney and one customs broker. Pull recent Chapter 7 and Subchapter V filings of importers and closed restaurants and send 300 letters offering no-win-no-fee reviews. Target 10 signed engagements and use the first recoveries as case studies.

title: Biotech Graveyard Data Exchange
one_liner: Rescue, clean and license the wet-lab data of shutting-down biotechs, especially the failed and negative results that AI drug-discovery models are starved of, and split the proceeds with the estate.
customer: AI-drug-discovery companies, big-pharma computational groups and ML-for-bio labs that license proprietary training data (ADME/tox, assay panels, SAR series, structural data). The sellers are wind-down estates, VCs and founders, who get a revenue share instead of paying anything.
problem: After the 2022-2025 biotech funding drought, hundreds of venture-backed biotechs have shut down or been hollowed out. When the last employee leaves, years of proprietary experimental data die on unpaid cloud accounts, expired ELN and LIMS licenses and laptops. Meanwhile AI models are trained on published literature, which is survivorship-biased: negative results almost never get published. Models lack the data on what does not work, and that data is exactly what dead companies hold.
solution: A wind-down data-salvage service, done in a 60-day window between the last payroll and server deletion. Triage what data exists and what is encumbered (licensor and CRO rights, academic-license terms). Extract from ELN, LIMS, instruments and cloud buckets. Limit the first scope to non-human-subject data such as biochemical and cell assays, chemistry, DMPK and structural data, so there is no PII problem. Get IP and rights sign-off from the estate or assignee. Standardize to a common assay schema with provenance. License as curated bundles to AI-bio and pharma buyers, with revenue flowing back to the estate.
why_now: The biotech shutdown and reverse-merger wave is in full swing, with wind-down specialists and startup shutdown services now established. AI-bio companies and pharma are openly competing for proprietary data, including federated and data-for-model-access programs. The 23andMe data-in-bankruptcy episode showed how badly data is currently handled in wind-downs. Cheap LLM-assisted schema mapping now makes normalizing messy legacy assay data affordable.
revenue_model: Free or low-cost triage for the estate. Take 30-50% of licensing revenue on each bundle, plus a fixed curation fee charged to buyers. Later, sell subscription access to a growing pooled 'negative results' corpus organized by target class.
non_obvious_insight: The dataset with the most scarcity value is the one everyone considers worthless: failed programs. Sellers are motivated because the alternative is deletion, and there is no consumer-privacy problem in assay data, unlike almost every other 'data for AI' market. The moat is trust and presence at the exact moment a company dies, meaning relationships with wind-down lawyers, biotech VCs and CFO-for-hire networks, not technology.
first_30_days: Reach out to 20 biotech VC platform partners, wind-down lawyers and fractional CFOs with a one-page offer of free data triage, revenue share and zero cost to the estate. Sign 2-3 shutting-down biotechs. Pre-sell sample packs to 3-5 AI-bio buyers and get a letter of intent on price per curated dataset. Build the minimal schema-normalization pipeline on the first dataset and get legal templates for estate-to-exchange licensing. Ship the first licensed bundle within the first 2-3 months.

title: Ex-Sales-Rep Route Collectives for Critical-Metal Scrap
one_liner: Commission-only teams of laid-off SDRs and inside-sales reps that each own a territory and sign machine shops and dental and electronics labs to take-back programs for tungsten carbide and cobalt scrap. Lots are aggregated and sold directly to domestic reclaimers.
customer: Sellers: tens of thousands of small generators such as machine and tool-and-die shops, carbide grinding shops and dental labs. Buyers: domestic carbide and tungsten reclaimers and refiners that now need US-allocated feedstock. Reps: displaced sales staff.
problem: The BIS rule restricts tungsten scrap exports and the DoD and DOE are subsidizing domestic supply, but supply is scattered across small generators who sell to local yards at a steep discount or trash the hard-to-value streams such as grinding swarf. The bottleneck is sales coverage of the long tail, not recovery technology. Entry-level SDR and BDR roles are among the first white-collar jobs AI is absorbing, leaving a large pool of trained cold-outreach talent.
solution: Each rep owns a metro territory and signs 30-100 shops to a free take-back program: lockable bins, an assay or XRF-based price sheet, payment by lot and simple compliance paperwork (including BIS and toll-processing documentation). Consolidate through partner yards or carriers and sell aggregated lots to reclaimers on term offtake. Start with carbide inserts and grinding swarf, then add cobalt-alloy turnings. Reps keep 15-25% of the net spread and a software backbone handles pricing, pickup scheduling and payouts.
why_now: The BIS allocation rule created a domestic-first buyer set. Machine shops are squeezed by tariffs and input costs and welcome found cash. SDR and entry-level sales roles are being cut in 2026 and reps are actively looking for commission work. The DOE ($134M) and DoD rare-earth and critical-mineral funding raise buyers' willingness to pay for documented domestic feed.
revenue_model: Spread on aggregated lots (buy at a fixed percentage of the reclaimer price and sell at the offtake price). Service fee on compliance paperwork. Later, SaaS for yards and reclaimers.
non_obvious_insight: In critical-material recycling the scarce resource is neither collection technology nor recovery chemistry but sales coverage of thousands of tiny generators. The people best at long-tail coverage are exactly the ones AI has just made cheap.
first_30_days: Pick one machine-shop-dense metro. Get a reclaimer to sign an offtake letter. Recruit five ex-SDRs and have them call 500 shops from public industrial directories. Collect and sell the first few tons of carbide and swarf, and document real price gaps versus the shops' current yards.

title: Supervised-Hours Bench for Counselors and Social Workers
one_liner: A managed group-supervision network and hour-logging platform that lets clinics fund the thousands of post-degree supervised hours gating counseling, MFT and social-work licenses.
customer: Group therapy practices, community mental-health agencies and school districts hiring associate-level counselors and social workers; the associates themselves.
problem: Counseling, psychology and social work were excluded from the higher federal loan cap. Licensure typically requires 2-4k supervised hours after the degree, and associates often pay $50-150 an hour out of pocket for supervision that is scarce and tracked on paper. Clinics cannot hire associates faster than supervisors can be found.
solution: Certified supervisors, often semi-retired licensed clinicians, deliver state-compliant group supervision by video. The platform logs hours in board-ready format and enforces state ratios and rules. Clinics pay per associate per month to onboard associates who can bill insurance under supervision.
why_now: The July 2026 loan caps squeeze students in excluded fields and push them toward employer support. Behavioral-health demand is high, and telesupervision is widely permitted in many states after the pandemic.
revenue_model: $150-300 per associate per month from the clinic, supervision delivery margin, and hour-logging SaaS. Optional share of billed associate revenue.
non_obvious_insight: The scarcest input in the credential chain is not the degree but post-degree supervision, and the payer is the employer, not the student, because associates bill insurance and become revenue-positive once supervised.
first_30_days: Pick one large state that permits telesupervision. Recruit 5 licensed supervisors. Sign 3 group practices with about 10 associates in total. Run the hour logs in spreadsheets first and charge $200 per associate per month. Verify board rules before selling.

title: Battery-Buffered Induction Kitchens for LPG-Starved Restaurants
one_liner: A load-sharing controller and optional battery lets Indian cloud kitchens and restaurants switch from scarce LPG to induction without waiting months for a utility load upgrade, then pools the fleet as a lunch-and-dinner-peak resource for DISCOMs.
customer: Cloud kitchens, small restaurant chains (5-50 outlets), hostel and office messes, caterers and sweet shops in Indian metros and tier-2 cities.
problem: The Hormuz-driven LPG shortage pushed induction cooktop demand up 20-25x and the government is distributing 500k stoves, but a commercial kitchen converting needs roughly 15-40 kW of extra connected load. DISCOM sanctioned-load upgrades and neighborhood transformers are slow and constrained, and the switch could add up to 27 GW of national demand at the evening peak. Low-income uptake is reported as sluggish because grid and financing are not ready.
solution: A CT-clamp controller (about $300-400) that sequences burners so total draw stays under the sanctioned load, since cooking tolerates duty-cycling. Add a 20-60 kWh LFP buffer to cover lunch and dinner peaks, financed as a monthly cooking-energy subscription through an NBFC and charged off-peak or on midday solar. The aggregated fleet later sells peak flexibility to DISCOMs under state demand-side management programs.
why_now: LPG scarcity is forcing commercial conversion now, stationary LFP packs are around $70/kWh, smart-meter and demand-side management programs are rolling out, and utilities cannot build capacity fast enough (transformer lead times, capex-biased regulation).
revenue_model: Controller sale of INR 25-35k, battery lease or subscription of roughly INR 15-30k per month (benchmarked against the commercial LPG bill it replaces, when LPG is available at all), and later DISCOM peak-flex payments per kW-year plus midday-charging arbitrage.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck to electrifying cooking is not the stove but the permission to draw power at the kitchen's meter. A battery and a scheduler turn an infrastructure-approval problem into a financing problem. Cooking is a rare thermal load that can be shaped without harming the product, so the cheap controller does most of the work and generates the data that later sells flexibility.
first_30_days: Sell 10 controllers to cloud kitchens in one metro through restaurant associations and cloud-kitchen operator WhatsApp groups. Log load data and outages, then lease batteries to the first 3 with an NBFC partner. Use the aggregated load data to open a sandbox conversation with one DISCOM.

title: Voucher Lease-Up Desk for Soft Markets
one_liner: An ops service that gets units voucher-ready and through housing-authority inspection and paperwork in days, turning Section 8 from a hassle into the cheapest demand source in a soft market.
customer: Mid-size multifamily operators (300-5,000 units) in soft Sun Belt markets with high concessions, with housing authorities and mobility nonprofits as secondary payers.
problem: Apartment List shows 7.0% vacancy, 34 days to lease (longest September since 2019) and concessions on 15.8% of stabilized units (Austin 37%). Yet many operators still avoid Housing Choice Voucher applicants because inspection scheduling and contract paperwork can stretch weeks, costing roughly $300+ of rent a week on a $1,388 median unit. Voucher holders, meanwhile, fail to find units.
solution: A virtual pre-inspection app that walks site staff through HUD's NSPIRE-based checklist with photos so units pass first time. It automates the tenancy-approval and contract packet and tracks status across 50-100 local housing authorities, checks rent-reasonableness and payment standards before pricing, and publishes a live 'voucher-ready units' feed to caseworkers.
why_now: Time-to-lease is at a multi-year high and concessions are replacing rent growth, so landlords will trade a small admin burden for near-guaranteed rent. Authority inspections have moved to one federal standard, which a checklist app can encode.
revenue_model: $350-600 per successful voucher lease-up (against a $1,400 month of vacancy) or $1.50 per unit per month subscription, plus contracts with authorities and mobility programs.
non_obvious_insight: Operators treat vouchers as a risk problem when it is a cycle-time problem, measured in days, which is exactly what a 34-day-to-lease market prices. Government pays most of the rent, so the lowest-CAC tenant class is being left on the table. Housing-authority funding stress is the main risk, so sell to authorities with reserves and use source-of-income laws as a second wedge.
first_30_days: Pick two metros. Call 20 regional managers and offer a free pre-inspection pilot on 10 vacant units. Partner with two authority landlord-liaison offices and one mobility nonprofit. Charge only per lease-up once the unit is under contract with the authority.

title: Independent Auditor for AI-Scribed Billing
one_liner: A continuous, coder-signed check on whether ambient AI scribe notes actually support the E/M levels being billed, before the payers or the government find out.
customer: Compliance officers, CFOs and revenue-integrity leaders at health systems and physician groups (20-500 providers), MSOs and PE-backed groups that rolled out ambient AI scribes. Secondary buyer: acquirers doing diligence on scribe-enabled practices.
problem: After ambient scribe rollouts, E/M distributions shift toward 99204-5 and 99214-5. Studies of six health systems show high-acuity visit share up roughly 12-20 points for new visits. Payers respond with AI downcoding and record requests, and the False Claims Act exposure is real if notes carry exam elements or time statements that did not happen. The scribe vendor cannot credibly audit itself, and annual compliance audits of 5-10 charts per provider cannot see systemic drift.
solution: Step 1 is a claims-only drift diagnostic (no EHR integration): compare each provider's E/M and modifier distribution before and after go-live with specialty benchmarks and peers, and rank the provider outliers. Step 2 is a targeted sample review by certified coders of the flagged encounters, checking that MDM or total-time really support the level. Copied-forward text, unsupported time attestations and orders without documented reasoning are the failure patterns. Step 3 is a continuing dashboard plus quarterly audit memos designed to be shown to a payer, auditor or the OIG. It includes a payer downcoding forecast.
why_now: Ambient scribes went mainstream across health systems in 2025-26. Research is documenting the coding-intensity increase and describing a payer-provider 'coding arms race', and payers are turning to their own AI for downcoding. The OIG's compliance program guidance expects organizations to audit new technology used in billing. Nobody independent has a standard offering yet.
revenue_model: $8-15 per audited encounter, or $15-30 per provider per month for the drift monitor plus sampled audits. Enterprise annual contracts of $50-200k. Diligence engagements at $10-25k each.
non_obvious_insight: The risk is not template bloat that scribes create in the HPI and exam. Under the 2021 E/M rules those elements do not count toward the level. The risk is that the scribe's fluent narration makes medical decision making and time statements sound stronger than what the physician did, and audits succeed or fail on MDM and time. Only coders who have survived payer audits know this. That is why a coder-signed audit is worth more than a model score, and why a compliance officer needs a third party, not the scribe vendor's coding module.
first_30_days: Find 3 mid-size groups, ideally with 30-100 providers, that adopted a scribe in the last 12 months, through LinkedIn outreach to compliance and revenue-integrity leads. Offer a free claims-only drift diagnostic, since 12 months of CPT data from their billing system is enough. Show them the outlier providers. Convert to a paid sample-audit engagement ($10-25k) and a monthly monitor. Recruit two certified auditors (CPC, CPMA) as contractors.

title: Post-Mortem CT Plus Remote Pathology for Coroners
one_liner: Give rural coroners a scan-and-remote-read pathway so cause-of-death answers arrive in a day instead of weeks, without buying a single scanner.
customer: County coroners and medical examiners in rural or under-resourced jurisdictions, state ME systems, and hospitals with after-hours CT capacity.
problem: There is a well-documented shortage of forensic pathologists. Many rural coroners are elected non-physicians, autopsies are outsourced hundreds of miles away with multi-week backlogs, and each autopsy costs thousands. Families can't finalize burial or estates without a death certificate.
solution: A protocol in which the body is scanned on a hospital CT off-hours (or a mobile unit), with external-exam photos uploaded to a network of board-certified forensic pathologists and radiologists. AI triage flags fractures, hemorrhage and foreign objects, and the coroner gets a 24-hour read with a recommendation on whether a full autopsy is needed. The coroner keeps statutory authority.
why_now: Post-mortem CT is routine in several countries, imaging AI has matured, and telepathology infrastructure exists. The forensic pathology shortage persists, and overdose and heat deaths have strained offices.
revenue_model: $600-$1,200 per case plus $30-$60K/year county retainers, with rental fees to hospitals for scanner time.
non_obvious_insight: The slowest step in death care isn't the funeral, it's the death certificate, and each day of delay costs families and insurers. A software-plus-network layer can loosen the choke point without owning capital equipment.
first_30_days: Recruit 3-5 forensic pathologists (retired or part-time) as remote readers. Approach 5 backlogged rural coroners and one rural hospital about a pilot. Expect pilot signing within 6 months, with full revenue closer to 12.

title: Used-Satellite Exchange With Independent Health Reports
one_liner: A broker and due-diligence shop that turns dead or distressed operators' on-orbit assets into sellable, verified inventory.
customer: Buyers: acquirers of the Rocket Lab type, infrastructure and PE funds, and governments or startups that want a quick constellation. Sellers: bankruptcy trustees, venture-debt lenders, insurers and cash-strapped first-generation smallsat operators.
problem: Insiders assume a satellite is worthless when its company dies. But the bus, license, orbit and customer contracts can still hold value, and buyers cannot verify condition. Lenders have no repossession or title process, and every M&A team improvises technical diligence.
solution: Two products. (1) An independent 'fleet health report' built from open orbital data (maneuver history, decay, propulsion-use proxies, beacon and telemetry checks) plus data-room review. (2) A brokerage that matches on-orbit assets and licenses to buyers, with regulator-approved license transfers handled by counsel.
why_now: Rocket Lab's roughly $8B Iridium deal and its CFO's 'more M&A' comment show on-orbit assets are being priced. 4,517 satellites deployed in 2025 means a large aging first-generation cohort. Funding is bifurcating into nine-figure rounds for a few winners and starvation for the rest.
revenue_model: $25-100k per health report. 3-8% success fee on brokered deals. Annual subscription for lenders and insurers who want portfolio monitoring.
non_obvious_insight: In space, value sits in the license, the orbit and the operating bus, and none of the three dies with the company. The missing piece is trusted third-party verification, which is a service business rather than a rocket business.
first_30_days: Publish free health scorecards on 20 public constellations to build credibility. Interview five venture-debt lenders and two space insurers about their current diligence. Sell two paid reports to funds looking at consolidation targets. Ask trustees of failed smallsat companies to list assets with you.

title: Fraud-Proof Sourcing for the Dye-and-Whey Scramble
one_liner: A concierge service that authenticates certificates of analysis, brokers and supplier identities for supply-short ingredients such as natural colors and whey.
customer: Procurement and QA or regulatory teams at $50M-3B food, beverage and private-label manufacturers reformulating away from petroleum dyes (Walmart private label dye-free in Jan 2027, FDA target Dec 2027) or scrambling for whey.
problem: Natural colorant demand is projected to rise 400-500%, the US is 98% import-dependent for annatto, and reformulation costs $50K-500K per SKU over 12-24+ months. Whey concentrate is up 108% in two years and some suppliers are sold out through 2026. Shortages under deadline pressure bring new brokers, prepayment demands and adulteration risk. Generative AI makes certificates of analysis, lab letterheads and audit certificates trivial to forge, and QA teams verify by email.
solution: For each lot: a direct callback or API check with the issuing lab (signed lab-issued COAs where possible), document forensics (metadata, accreditation numbers versus registries), supplier identity and beneficial-owner checks, bank-account-name match to catch payment redirection, and importer-chain (FSVP) checks. Members contribute data to a pooled adulteration signature library (chromatography and spectral patterns) that becomes the moat.
why_now: Two hard deadlines (Walmart Jan 2027, FDA Dec 2027) and a whey shortage are forcing buyers to source from unfamiliar suppliers now. More than 70 alt-protein companies have folded or been acquired since September 2024, so distressed ingredient stock is moving through brokers. Forging documents with AI is now near-free.
revenue_model: $250-600 per verified lot on a concierge basis, then $2-6K a month subscriptions for monitoring and access to the member data pool, plus lab referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: In shortages the fraudster's edge is paperwork, not chemistry. Buyers under deadline pressure waive diligence. A KYC layer that never touches a molecule but is bonded to accredited labs can become the trust network, and the pooled fingerprint library gets more valuable with every member.
first_30_days: Reach 10 QA directors on LinkedIn. Offer the first 5 COA verifications free in exchange for lot data. Sign 2 accredited labs for callback verification. Publish a one-page 'natural color and whey counterfeits to watch' guide for lead generation. Convert 3 pilots at about $2,500 each.

title: Serial-Level Collateral Registry for GPU Lenders
one_liner: The independent field-exam firm and cross-lender double-pledge registry for AI hardware debt, built on the military rule that a serial number appears on one hand receipt only.
customer: Private-credit funds, banks, equipment lessors, ABS trustees and insurers financing neocloud GPU fleets, which now hold well over $20 billion in GPU-backed debt. Secondary: neoclouds that need audit-ready proof to borrow at lower spreads.
problem: Lenders rely on borrower-supplied serial lists, telemetry and occasional inspections. After the Tricolor and First Brands double-pledging scandals (the SEC charged Tricolor's former executives in August 2026), lenders know 'the same collateral pledged twice' is real. GPU servers sit in multi-tenant colocation halls, are easy to move, swap or re-pledge to another SPV, and telemetry can be spoofed. Serial-number UCC filings are rarely searched across lenders, and a colo technician paid by the borrower is not an independent counter.
solution: Three layers. (1) A repeatable two-person independent inventory protocol: witnessed reads of chassis label, BMC out-of-band serial and GPU-level serial, plus rack and cage photos, location and power draw. (2) Serialized tamper-evident seals on cages and rack doors, checked at each visit. (3) A privacy-preserving cross-lender registry of hashed serials so a lender learns whether a serial is already pledged elsewhere without revealing its book. Deliver monthly compliance packages that plug into the loan's reporting covenants for the trustee.
why_now: GPU-backed lending crossed $20 billion, and CoreWeave's $8.5 billion delayed-draw term loan (March 2026) showed the asset class reaching investment-grade structures. Tricolor and First Brands made 'verify the collateral independently' a board-level demand in private credit. Loan documents already grant lenders inspection rights, so the buyer has the access but not the in-house field-exam capability. Export-control diversion risk adds a second reason for chain-of-custody evidence.
revenue_model: Per-site audit of $15-50k, annual monitoring retainer of $50-250k per facility, registry subscriptions of $50-200k per lender, and trustee or insurer reporting packages. Long-term, per-basis-point fees on financed collateral under verification.
non_obvious_insight: Fraud lives at the seam between paper and physical, and the only reliable control is a count by someone who does not report to the borrower. That is what a military property book officer and a sensitive-item inventory do. Lenders will not share collateral lists with each other but will share hashes to avoid being second in line, so the registry becomes the moat. Telemetry proves a box is powered on, not that it is the box you financed.
first_30_days: Recruit 2-3 former property book or supply officers plus a data-center operations technician. Write and publish the audit protocol. Approach 5 mid-tier credit funds and equipment lenders (not the giants) that do GPU deals and lack field-exam staff. Offer a fixed-fee pilot audit on a live deal using the lender's existing inspection rights. Get a securities and privacy lawyer to bless the hashed-serial registry design before any lender data is pooled.

title: Buy the Orphaned License of Dead Models
one_liner: Acquire or secure exclusive commercial-licensing rights to hugely downloaded open models and tools whose company died, then sell clean, warranted commercial licenses plus a public orphan-license registry.
customer: Startups and mid-size companies shipping voice features (dubbing, audiobooks, IVR, game NPC voices, accessibility) on top of XTTS-class models, and the procurement or legal teams of their enterprise buyers who now ask for model-license provenance.
problem: Coqui XTTS-v2 is still pulled about 6.75M times a month under a non-commercial license (CPML), but Coqui shut down in Dec 2023. Commercial licensing was 'available upon inquiry' from a company that no longer exists, so builders either violate the license, ship legal risk to customers, or rip out the best multilingual voice-cloning model. GitHub threads asking about commercial use or the license after shutdown were closed 'wontfix'.
solution: Phase 1: trace the rights chain (Coqui Inc., founders, assignees, any bankruptcy or dissolution filings) and option an exclusive commercial-licensing agency deal or outright IP purchase, which should be cheap because the seller is a dead startup. Phase 2: sell per-product annual commercial licenses ($2k-$25k) with a written rights-chain warranty and an audit letter that customers can hand to enterprise procurement. Phase 3: publish an Orphan Model Registry (model, steward status, license, who can grant commercial rights) as a free lead-gen asset and a paid API for AI-governance tools. Fallback if the rights-holder refuses: sell a fixed-price license-risk audit and a swap-to-permissive-model migration (Apache/MIT TTS) with regression tests.
why_now: Enterprise AI-governance questionnaires in 2026 ask for model and data provenance. The $1.5B Anthropic authors settlement (2025) and the Authors Guild v. OpenAI/Microsoft unsealed briefs (HN front page 2026-09-27, 626 points) made license hygiene a board-level topic. Open voice tools are exploding: VoiceStudio hit 43.9k stars, +27k in one month, and its README warns each bundled model has its own license to review before commercial use.
revenue_model: Annual per-product licenses ($2k-$25k), enterprise-wide licenses, audit and migration fees ($3k-$8k fixed price), registry API subscription ($200-$1k a month).
non_obvious_insight: Demand is already proven and supply is literally zero: nobody can sell a commercial license because the seller is dead, so dead-startup IP is the scarcest cheap asset in open AI. Evidence: XTTS-v2 shows 6,752,613 downloads last month under CPML (https://huggingface.co/coqui/XTTS-v2). Coqui repo issues on commercial use, license after shutdown and 'Move to MIT' are closed wontfix (https://github.com/coqui-ai/TTS/issues?q=commercial+license+is%3Aissue). Issue #4022, opened nearly a year after shutdown, says the community is confused about 'commercial use and fine-tuning' (https://github.com/coqui-ai/TTS/issues/4022). HN, Nov 2023: XTTS stays non-commercial with commercial licensing 'upon inquiry'. VoiceStudio's AGPL repo warns model licenses vary (https://github.com/debpalash/VoiceStudio).
first_30_days: Days 1-7: pull Delaware and other corporate records for Coqui Inc., message the founders and former staff, and draft a one-page option agreement (small cash plus revenue share). Days 1-10: build the registry from 50 popular non-commercial or orphaned models on Hugging Face. Days 10-30: email companies that opened XTTS licensing issues and companies whose products visibly use XTTS (from public GitHub dependency graphs) with a $3k risk audit, and aim for 3-5 paid audits. If the rights option lands, convert those audits into licenses.

title: Distributor Credit Radar for Failing Restaurants
one_liner: A weekly early-warning score on each restaurant account, built from public signals and distributors' own order and payment data, so food distributors can tighten terms before the customer goes dark.
customer: Independent foodservice distributors (produce, protein, dairy, beverage, paper) with $20-500M in revenue that sell on net-14 and net-30 terms to restaurants. The buyer is the credit manager, controller or owner.
problem: Restaurants are high-turnover, thinly capitalized credit risks, and distributors are unsecured creditors who see the problem last. Generic credit bureaus are weak on restaurants. When consumer spending is squeezed and rates are higher, bad debt climbs and distributors respond with blunt tools (COD for everyone) that lose good accounts.
solution: A risk score per account, refreshed weekly, combining health-inspection trends, permit and liquor-license status, lien and judgment filings, review and hours changes, delivery-platform activity, foot traffic, and the distributor's own signals (order-size decline, days-to-pay drift). Alerts recommend cutting limits, switching to COD or accelerating collection. A consortium data pool of anonymized payment experience improves the score for every member. A bad-debt shield insurance product can follow.
why_now: Squeezed lower-income consumers, higher borrowing costs and the energy-cost shock raise restaurant failures. Public and alternative data on restaurants is now cheap to assemble, and distributors are digitizing accounts receivable and order data.
revenue_model: $600-2,500 per month per distributor by account count, plus consortium data access and later an insurance referral share.
non_obvious_insight: Restaurants fail visibly weeks or months before they stop paying. The best predictor is the distributor's own order-size decline, which they are not analyzing, and the consortium effect (shared payment behavior) becomes a data moat no single distributor can build.
first_30_days: Get three regional distributors to share two years of anonymized accounts-receivable history and back-test whether public signals warn 8-12 weeks before write-offs. Sell a paid pilot at $1,500 per month. Each avoided $20k write-off pays for the subscription for a year.

title: Managed Runtime for Custom Apps Built for Local Businesses
one_liner: A white-label hosting, backup and "someone to call" layer for AI-built custom apps that freelancers and owners now build for small businesses.
customer: Two buyers. (a) Solo builders, freelancers and small agencies who build custom tools for local businesses, including failed micro-SaaS founders. They pay wholesale per app and mark it up. (b) Small business owners who built a tool themselves and want it kept alive.
problem: Builders and buyers have both moved off subscription SaaS, and reliability is now nobody's job. r/SaaS: "Customer cancelled after 18 months. Reason: 'We built it ourselves.'", "No one is going to pay for your vibe-coded SaaS", "Mass-produced AI apps for 14 months. Made $2,847 total. My friend sells pool cleaning services and cleared $94K.", "I wasted $50k because I thought the code was the expensive part." r/Entrepreneur (88/100): "The SaaS model is quietly falling apart for small businesses." When the dispatch board or intake form breaks at 7am, nobody is answerable.
solution: 1) A one-click deploy of an AI-built app to a hardened runtime with auth, nightly backups, uptime checks, data export and secrets rotation. 2) Dependency and security patching. 3) A "break-glass" human fix within one business day, sold as credits. 4) Builders resell the bundle with their own markup, so they earn recurring revenue from boring customers instead of chasing SaaS signups. 5) The small business gets an SLA and a runbook in plain language.
why_now: In February 2026 nearly $1T was wiped from software and services valuations as coding agents made build-versus-buy tilt toward build (TechCrunch, Mar 1, 2026). Small customers are now building their own replacements, and thousands of AI-SaaS founders who cannot sell subscriptions are turning to service-style custom work.
revenue_model: $39-79 per app per month wholesale to builders, who charge clients $100-200/mo. Break-glass fix credits ($150 per incident). A $199/mo direct plan for owners who built their own tool.
non_obvious_insight: When code is cheap, the scarce thing is accountability: someone who answers when the tool breaks. The supply and demand are visible in the same threads: small customers churn because they built it themselves (r/SaaS, https://www.ideafast.pro/pains/saas), and r/Entrepreneur scores "The SaaS model is quietly falling apart for small businesses" at 88/100 (https://www.ideafast.pro/pains/Entrepreneur). The macro shift toward build over buy is documented at https://techcrunch.com/2026/03/01/saas-in-saas-out-heres-whats-driving-the-saaspocalypse/. Honest caveat: the demand for the caretaking layer is inferred from these signals, not seen in a direct "I'd pay for" post, so the first month is a paid-demand test.
first_30_days: Week 1: DM 30 builders who posted about pivoting to "boring" service customers, and offer to host and maintain their existing client apps for $49. Weeks 2-3: onboard 10 real apps onto a standard stack (managed database, backups, uptime monitor, alerts) using off-the-shelf tooling. Week 4: sell the wholesale plan to the first 3 builders and log every incident to price break-glass credits. Kill test: fewer than 5 paying apps after 30 days means the pain is not there.

title: Birth Plan B for Maternity Deserts
one_liner: Carve the last three weeks of childbirth logistics out of the hospital: pre-booked lodging, ride dispatch, nurse triage and an emergency-delivery kit for mothers whose local labor ward closed.
customer: Payers: Medicaid managed-care plans and state programs spending Rural Health Transformation money, rural employers and self-insured plans, and mothers directly ($349 to $699). Users: pregnant women in maternity-desert counties.
problem: At least 96 hospital labor-and-delivery units closed across 35 states between 2024 and early 2026, and in nearly 60% of affected counties it was the only birthing facility. About one in three US counties is a maternity-care desert, and more Medicaid cuts starting in 2027 are expected to close more units. Families improvise the final weeks: a 60 to 90 minute drive, no place to stay at 39 weeks, a partner who cannot leave work, and unplanned roadside births.
solution: A subscription from week 34. It includes choosing and pre-registering a receiving hospital, plus a contracted hotel or extended-stay room within 15 minutes of that hospital, for the 38 to 41 week window or triggered at first contractions. It adds on-call ride dispatch through a local non-emergency medical transport or taxi operator, with backup childcare and pet care. A 24/7 OB-nurse triage line (a telehealth partner) decides between go now and wait. The kit includes emergency-birth supplies and a 45-minute partner class coordinated with local EMS, and it ends with a return ride and first-week check-ins. No clinical license is needed because it wraps logistics around existing care.
why_now: CMS awarded the $50B Rural Health Transformation Program to all 50 states on December 29, 2025 (about $200M per state in year one). 35 state applications include maternal or child health, several include obstetric transport, and states face an October 30, 2026 deadline to obligate first-year awards. That makes subcontractors with a concrete pilot unusually welcome right now.
revenue_model: A per-member-per-pregnancy fee of roughly $300 to $900 from Medicaid managed-care plans as a value-added benefit, or a state RHTP subaward. Consumer self-pay of $349 to $699. Employer add-on for rural self-insured plans. Margin on lodging and rides.
non_obvious_insight: When a unit closes, the hospital's cost disappears and the family's cost explodes in the final three weeks. The fix is logistics (room blocks, dispatch, triage), which a non-clinical startup can assemble in weeks. Medicaid finances roughly four in ten US births and already pays for non-emergency transport, so the payer exists. The wedge is packaging this as a contractable benefit plans can add, with roadside-birth and ED-bypass metrics as proof.
first_30_days: Pick one closure county in the news and its receiving hospital 45 to 90 minutes away. Contract 6 discounted extended-stay rooms, one local transport operator and a telehealth OB-nurse line. Pilot with 20 mothers via the county health department, WIC and rural clinics, priced at cost or free. Log outcomes. Pitch two Medicaid plans' value-added-benefit teams and the state RHTP office with the pilot data and a one-page subaward proposal before the October 30 obligation deadline. In parallel, sell the consumer version through rural parenting groups, churches and doulas.
